The modulator section offers six presets: triangle, sawtooth, sine, square, ramp up, and ramp down. There's also a custom mode that lets you type a 32-step opcode sequence directly as text, using numbers from 0 to 7.

On top of that, it includes LFO, FM, and off modulation modes, ADSR envelopes for both the carrier and modulator, velocity and pitch bend support, and a switchable low-pass filter modeled on the original hardware's roughly 2kHz output filter. The interface is split into three sections: Global, Carrier, and Modulator. Global handles gain, polyphony, pitch bend range, theme, preset loading, and the hardware-style low-pass filter, while the lower half is where you shape the carrier waveform and modulation behavior.

Magical FDS Plug is open source, released under the GPLv3 license, with its source code posted on GitHub. The download also includes demo presets that keep the FDS parts of YMCK's demo songs intact. It runs as AU and VST3 on macOS 10.13 and up, and as VST3 on Windows.
AI-made music has quietly moved from a novelty into a real operational challenge.

Over the past year, the conversation around AI music has moved beyond questions of creativity or copyright. For streaming platforms, distributors, labels, publishers, and rights organizations, the more urgent concern turns out to be practical: how do you even tell whether a track was made by a human, by AI, or by some mix of both?

As the volume of AI music keeps growing, that question gets harder to ignore. According to figures from the streaming service Deezer, the platform now receives roughly 75,000 fully AI-generated tracks a day, a substantial share of all the music uploaded to the service.

This week, Boston-based audio intelligence company Modulate unveiled a new AI music detection API. Rather than relying only on metadata or creators' self-disclosure, the tool helps music platforms identify AI vocals and instrumentation directly from the audio file.

Many companies have so far leaned on transparency policies, under which artists, labels, or distributors disclose AI involvement themselves. But "there is a growing recognition that self-disclosure alone may not be enough." As AI music generation tools become easier for anyone to use, platforms are increasingly looking for ways to independently verify the tracks they receive.

Modulate says its system analyzes music by separating out vocals and instrumentation to look for signs of AI generation. Rather than a simple yes-or-no, it produces segment-by-segment verdicts. The company argues this level of granularity is needed as the industry moves away from the idea that every track can be neatly sorted into either human or AI.

The technology arrives amid growing concern over streaming fraud. Industry figures point out that AI tools have made it easier than ever to mass-produce tracks, which can then be uploaded and used for fraudulent streaming.

Of course, detection technology alone does not resolve every challenge AI poses for the music industry. Questions around copyright, attribution, licensing, and artist consent remain unsettled. Still, as AI music takes up a growing share of the ecosystem, many stakeholders have begun to see detection not as a peripheral feature but as foundational infrastructure.

For independent artists, the issue is less about whether AI should be allowed into music-making at all, and more about how to prove a genuine creator hasn't been drowned out in an increasingly crowded sea of synthetic tracks.

This is a video from YouTuber Songs by Spencer. True to its title, 'Suno Helped Me Write a BETTER Song,' he tests firsthand whether AI can really help write a better song. He starts with a simple acoustic demo.

He runs this demo through Suno AI. Rather than using the output as is, he treats it as a starting point for inspiration and remakes the song into a completely new version, layering human judgment on top of the AI's draft.
Throughout the video, he walks through how he uses AI music tools: sparking creative ideas, breaking through lyric writer's block, and raising the quality of songwriting and production.

This video is for anyone curious about AI, music, songwriting, or tools like Suno. It follows one creator's real workflow, bringing AI in as a songwriting partner while leaving the final polish to a human.
On Thursday, June 25, Suno launched a new artist incubator program called Spark. It gives selected independent artists grants and marketing support, and opens a path into Suno's songwriting camps.

Participating artists retain full creative control and commercial rights to their work. According to Suno, grant amounts vary depending on where an artist is in their career and can range from a few thousand dollars to tens of thousands. Marketing support is also tailored to each artist's needs, spanning influencer marketing and advertising, digital exposure, visual and art production, events and activations, and press opportunities.
Suno made clear it does not get involved in choosing or using a distributor. That decision is left entirely up to the artist.

"Emerging artists tell us the same thing again and again: tools alone aren't enough. They need support and exposure," Suno Chief Music Officer Paul Sinclair and Rosie Nguyen, head of creative economy and monetization, wrote in a blog post. "Spark's goal is to help more artists grow an idea into a finished project, connect that project with fans, and create new opportunities to build a career both on and off Suno."
Eligibility comes down to three conditions: being 18 or older, being a singer, songwriter, or producer releasing music under their own name, and being an independent artist.

Over the past year, Suno's songwriting camps have become a key channel for reaching music talent and introducing them to the generative AI product, which creates songs from scratch using nothing more than a simple text prompt. In January, the company invited Billboard to a private studio camp session in Los Angeles that included Timbaland, as well as Ommas Keith (Frank Ocean, Erykah Badu, Jay-Z) and Gino The Ghost (Sabrina Carpenter, The Chainsmokers, Saweetie). At the camp, experts used Suno to capture a song idea, then human musicians reworked the material piece by piece, adding their own improvisation and style.

On an episode of Billboard on the Record, Suno CEO Mikey Shulman was asked whether the company plans to become a record label. He answered: "No. We're thinking about building a music super app. A record label is a separate thing from that."

The program arrives just weeks after Suno announced a $400 million Series D round led by Bond Capital, which valued the company at $5.4 billion post-money. Separate from investor confidence, Suno continues to face copyright infringement claims from music industry incumbents.

Suno is currently facing a $500 million copyright infringement lawsuit from Universal Music Group and Sony Music. The major labels allege Suno trained on their copyrighted recordings without proper consent or authorization. (Warner Music Group was once part of the suit as well, but dropped out after settling and signing a licensing deal with Suno in late 2025.) German copyright group GEMA and Danish copyright group Koda are also each pursuing their own copyright infringement lawsuits against Suno.

This week, national class-action law firm Hagens Berman joined a lawsuit brought by independent artists who claim their copyrighted music was used to train Suno's models without authorization, infringing their copyrights.
